prompt:
Role and task instructions:
You are a helpful, respectful and honest assistant.

User request:
[Goal] Practice playing the instrument.
[Condition] You are unable to read sheet music
[Initial plan] Choose an Instrument > Learn Basic Terminology > Start with Simple Songs > Experiment with Melodies > Stay Consistent
[Problem] You find the plan quite vague and miss necessary steps.

For a given goal, make the plan more comprehensive and concrete. For each step you plan to take, mark with '[Step xx]'.
answer:
[Step 01] Choose one instrument.
Pick an instrument you enjoy hearing and can access regularly. Consider cost, space, noise, and physical comfort. If undecided, try two or three instruments at a music shop or borrow one before buying.

[Step 02] Set a specific first goal.
For example: “Within four weeks, I will play a simple, familiar song from beginning to end at a steady, comfortable speed.” Choose a short song with a repeating melody or a few chords.

[Step 03] Prepare your instrument and practice space.
Get the essential accessories for your instrument, such as a tuner, picks, or an adjustable bench. Keep the instrument easy to reach and set aside a quiet practice spot. Learn how to tune it if needed.

[Step 04] Choose learning materials that do not require sheet music.
Find a beginner course using demonstrations, recordings, or visual guides. Guitar tablature, keyboard diagrams, and numbered fingering guides can help. Choose one main course so your lessons follow a consistent order.

[Step 05] Learn the essential terminology.
Start with beat, rhythm, tempo, pitch, melody, and chord. Learn the names of your instrument’s main parts and how its strings, keys, or playing surfaces are identified. Connect each term to something you can hear or demonstrate.

[Step 06] Establish comfortable playing technique.
Use an instrument-specific beginner lesson to learn posture, hand position, and how to produce a clear sound. Practice for five minutes at a time, staying relaxed. Stop and adjust if playing causes pain; seek feedback if discomfort continues.

[Step 07] Practice keeping a steady beat.
Clap or tap along to a familiar song. Then use a metronome at a comfortable speed, such as 60 beats per minute, and make one sound per click. Aim for 30 seconds without losing the beat before trying two sounds per click.

[Step 08] Learn a small set of useful sounds.
Learn only what your first song needs: perhaps three chords, five melody notes, or one basic drum pattern. Practice each sound slowly, then practice switching between them. Prioritize clear, relaxed playing.

[Step 09] Learn your first song in small sections.
Listen to the song, hum its melody, and use a demonstration or visual guide to learn a short phrase. Repeat that phrase slowly until you can play it correctly three times, then add the next phrase.

[Step 10] Connect sections and repair difficult transitions.
Join two learned phrases together. If you repeatedly stumble, isolate the last few sounds of the first phrase and the first few of the next. Practice that transition slowly before returning to the whole section.

[Step 11] Train your ear and experiment.
Spend three minutes finding a familiar tune by trial and error. Sing a short phrase, then search for matching sounds on your instrument. Also invent a short melody or rhythm using sounds you already know.

[Step 12] Follow a repeatable practice routine.
Practice for 20 minutes, five days a week: three minutes warming up, four minutes on rhythm or technique, ten minutes on your song, and three minutes experimenting. On busy days, do a focused five-minute session.

[Step 13] Record and review your progress weekly.
Record one uninterrupted attempt at your song. Listen for steady timing, clear sounds, and smooth transitions. Note one improvement and one specific problem to work on next. A teacher or experienced player can help check your technique.

[Step 14] Finish the first goal and increase difficulty gradually.
Once you can play the song through at a steady speed, choose another that adds one new skill, such as a new chord or rhythm. Keep revisiting earlier songs, and adjust your timeline if you need more practice.
